column2: A man with much wind (vata) is fickle, irascible, timid, talkative, fond of quarrels, and in dreams he moves through the sky.
A man with much bile (pitta) goes grey before his time, is quick to anger, very wise, fond of battle, and in dreams sees bright things.
A man with much phlegm (kapha) has steady friends, steady zeal, a firm body, and wealth; in dreams he sees water and white things.
The fluid (rasa) in the bodies of beings gives life; so does blood, which sustains; flesh is what coats the body, and fat produces unctuousness.
Bone is what supports; marrow is what fills and increases vigour; "ojas" makes semen and vigour, sustains the vital breath and the life's stability.
Ojas, more essential than semen, is taken in and reaches the heart. The body is said to have six parts: thighs, arms, head, and belly.
There are six layers of skin: the outer one, another that holds blood, another that holds delight (or sweat), and a fourth that holds ulcers (kunda).
The fifth is the seat of abscesses; the sixth is held to support life; the seventh layers support flesh; the second holds blood.

Another rests on the liver and spleen; one holds fat and bone; there is a layer for marrow, phlegm and faeces, situated in the digestive receptacle; the sixth holds bile; another holds semen, in the seat of semen.
Knowers of the Veda say that women have three "vyamas" (spans) too; from the union of blood and wind arises the womb.
From the spreading of phlegm the heart arises, like a lotus, facing downward and hollow, where the soul is established.
All states of being, following consciousness, are established there. On its left is the spleen, and on its right the liver.
On the right is the lung, so the lotus (heart) is described. The channels in this body that carry phlegm and blood...
...from inferring their elements, the senses arise. The white circle of the eyes is born of phlegm and comes from the father.
The dark circle comes from wind and comes from the mother; the circle of skin, it should be known, comes from mother and father together.
The tongue is born of flesh, blood and phlegm; fat is born of blood, phlegm and flesh; the testicles are known; these are the ten seats of life.
The head, heart, navel, throat, tongue, semen, blood, anus, bladder and ankle — sixteen are named.
Two hands, two feet, and four at the back of the neck: in the body, from foot to head, there are sixteen nets (tendon-networks).
Of flesh, sinew, vessel and bone there are four each, separately, fastened together at the wrists and ankles.
Six "kurcas" (bundles) are mentioned here: in the two hands, the two feet separately, in the neck and in the organ of generation, as the wise have said.
Four cords of flesh run along the spine; and ninety muscles are the binders of them.
Seven sutures and five lie about the head; one each belongs to the organ and the tongue; the bones number three hundred and sixty.
With the small ones, sixty-four teeth (bones) and twenty nails; the rods of the hands and feet; four places belong to them.
Sixty finger bones; two in the heels and four in the ankles; four in each forearm, and likewise in the shanks.
Two each in the knees, cheek, thigh, and shoulder-blade; so one should describe the eye-socket, shoulder, hip and pelvis bones.
Pelvis-bones a few, and in the back forty-five; in the neck are the bones, and the collar-bone and the jaw.
Its root two; the forehead, eyes, cheeks, nose and chin are set; ribs with palate-bones and the small joints make seventy-two.
Two in the temples; the skull has four plates; the chest seventeen bones; the joints number two hundred and ten.
In the limbs sixty-eight, and fifty-nine; within, eighty-three; and nine hundred sinews.
Two hundred and thirty... in the inner region seventy; the upward ones are six hundred; the branches are thus described.
Five hundred muscles; forty going upward; four hundred in the limbs and sixty within.
In women there are twenty more, then four; ten in the breasts, thirteen in the womb and the receptacle.
And four for the embryo; of the vessels of embodied beings there are thirty hundred-thousands and nine others.
Fifty-six thousand carry the fluid in the body, like channels in a field; and what is moisture, ointments and the like...
Seventy-two crores of openings here, O great sage; of marrow, fat, and also of serum...
...of urine, bile, phlegm, faeces, blood and lymph, the quantities are held in order to be handfuls ("anjali").
Each is taken as half again more than the preceding handful; half a handful of semen, and half of that of ojas.
And the wise have said four for the menses of women. Knowing the body as a lump of impurities and faults, one should relinquish it in the Self.
I shall tell of the hells where sinners suffer, and of those torments. Below the earth there are twenty-eight crores of hells.
They lie at the end of the seventh nether region, in dread darkness. The first crore is called Ghora; below it is Sughora.
Then Atighora, Mahaghora, the fifth Ghorarupa; the sixth called Taralatara; the seventh Bhayanaka.
Bhayotkata, Kalaratri, Mahachanda, Chandaya, Kolahala, Prachanda, Padma — leader of the hells.
Padmavati, Bhishana, Bhima, Karalika, Vikarala, Mahavajra, Trikona, Panchakonika.
Sadirgha, Vartula, Saptabhuma, Subhumika, Diptamaya — twenty-eight crores, giving sinners pain.
Of the twenty-eight crores there are five leaders each; Raurava and the others number one hundred and forty-four.
Tamisra, Andhatamisra, Maharaurava, Raurava, Asipatravana, and Lohabhara.
Naraka, Kalasutra, Mahanaraka; Sanjivana, Mahavichi, Tapana, Sampratapana.
Sanghata, Sakakola, Kudmala, Putimrittika, Lohashanku, Rijisha, Pradhana, and the Shalmali river.
Know these hells, lords of crores, terrible to look at; evildoers are cast into them, many into each one.
They have faces of cats, owls, jackals, vultures and the like; they throw a man into a trough of oil and kindle a fire.
Others are placed in frying-pans, others in copper vessels, others in iron vessels, and among many sparks of fire.
Others, set upon the points of spears, are pierced in hell; they are beaten with whips and made to eat balls of iron.
The servants of Yama make men eat dust, faeces, blood, phlegm and the like; they make them drink hot liquor, and tear men apart again.
They crush them in machines; they are devoured by crows and the like; they are sprinkled with hot oil and their heads are cut in many ways.
Crying "Alas, father!", they cut down their own deeds. Having reached the terrible, censured hells born of great sins...
...when their karma is exhausted, great sinners are born here. A slayer of a Brahmin takes the womb of a deer, dog, boar, or camel.
A drinker of liquor and a stealer of gold become ass, pukkasa, and mleccha; one who violates the teacher's bed becomes worm, insect, moth, grass, or shrub.
A slayer of a Brahmin has consumption; a drinker of liquor has black teeth; a gold-thief has bad nails; one who violates the teacher's bed has diseased skin.
Whoever consorts with these takes on his mark. A grain-thief becomes a cheat; a stealer of speech becomes dumb.
A thief of grain has a deformed body; a slanderer has a foul-smelling nose; an oil-thief drinks oil; an informer has a foul mouth.
One who steals another's wife and a Brahmin's property is born as a brahmarakshasa in a lonely forest.
A jewel-thief is of low birth; a thief of fragrances becomes a musk-rat; a stealer of leaves becomes a peacock; a stealer of grain a talker.
A thief of milk is a goat, a stealer of an animal a crow, of a vehicle a camel, of fruit a monkey, of honey a gadfly, of fruit a vulture, of utensils a house-crow.
A cloth-thief is a jackal; a stealer of salt a cricket. Thus are spoken the ills of the self (adhyatmika) and those from weapons and the like (adhibhautika).
Those from planets, fire, gods and the like are called adhidaivika. By knowledge and yoga one should destroy this threefold sorrow of samsara, and through penances, vows, gifts and worship of Vishnu.
Even those grown old in austerity and in years are bewildered by women. Liquor is known as threefold: gaudi, paishti and madhvi.
The fourth liquor, known as "woman", is that by which this world is infatuated: one is intoxicated by seeing a woman, but by drinking liquor.
Since a woman's glance is intoxicating, one should not look at her. A man who forcibly takes another's property, whatever it is...
...certainly becomes an animal, as does one who eats an unoffered oblation. One may accept a loincloth, a garment, a quilt against cold,
and sandals, but should make no hoard of anything else; only cloth and the like needed to sustain the body may be taken.
The body, joined with dharma, should be carefully protected. Purity is said to be of two kinds: outer and inner.
The outer is said to be by earth and water; the inner by purity of feeling. He who is pure in both is pure; none other is pure.
Contentment is said to be satisfaction with whatever comes. Concentration of mind and senses is said to be austerity.
Mastery of them is the highest dharma, above all dharmas. Austerity of speech is chanting mantras and the like; of mind, giving up passion;
of body, worship of the gods and the like — this is the threefold austerity. From the syllable Om come the Vedas, and the Vedas rest in Om.
